extracted.intended_audience: students, naturalists, and taxonomists studying freshwater sponges and hydrozoa
extracted.subtask_description: Morphological, ecological, and life-history criteria for describing and distinguishing freshwater sponges (Spongillidae) and hydrozoans (Hydra and related Coelenterata). Emphasis on anatomical characters (spicules, gemmules, body layers, nematocysts), measurements, habitat, behaviour and reproductive modes used in identification and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: External form and surface features (sponges)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sponge 'forms a thin but extremely hard and resistant crust the surface of which is either level, slightly concave, or distinctly corrugated; occasional groups of spicules project from it... The oscula are small; some of them are raised above the general surface but not on regular turret-shaped eminences. The colour is grey or black.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overall growth-form (thin crust, corrugated, raised oscula), presence/arrangement of projecting spicule-groups, and colour as diagnostic external characters; compare with closely related taxa (e.g., C. burmanica) where arrangement/regularity of projections differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeleton structure (sponges)
rubrics_metrics.description: The skeleton 'is extremely dense owing to the large number of spicules it contains, but almost structureless; broad vertical groups of spicules occur but lack spongin and only traverse a small part of the thickness of the sponge... At the base of the sponge the direction of a large proportion of the spicules is horizontal or nearly horizontal, the number arranged vertically being much greater in the upper part.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess density, presence/absence of spongin, organization into vertical groups, and predominant orientation of spicules through the thickness (horizontal at base, vertical above) when distinguishing species and interpreting mechanical properties (firmness due to interlocking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spicule morphology and measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Skeleton-spicules are 'sausage-shaped and often a little swollen at the ends or constricted in the middle... a few bear irregular projections or swellings. The majority, however, are quite smooth.' Amphistrongyli average ~0.28 × 0.024 mm; flesh-spicule shaft lengths cluster about 0.159 mm or about 0.05 mm; rotula diameter ~0.0106 mm with 6–8 spines; gemmule-spicules range from ~0.08 × 0.014 to 0.034 × 0.007 mm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record shape (sausage-shaped, swollen ends, twisted/bent), surface ornament (spines, smooth), and precise measurements (length × diameter) and note variability and intermediate forms; these quantitative spicule characters are primary diagnostic data in descriptions and comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule structure and layering
rubrics_metrics.description: Each gemmule 'is covered with a thick chitinous membrane in close contact with its wall... this membrane is full of spicules arranged as in a mosaic... Separated from this layer by a considerable interval is another layer of spicules embedded in a chitinous membrane... The membrane is in close contact with a dense cage of skeleton-spicules arranged parallel to it and bound together by chitinous substance... There is a single depressed aperture in the gemmules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe gemmule coverings (number of spicule-bearing layers, presence of a chitinous mosaic, intervening space), the cage of skeleton-spicules, and the position/shape of the aperture (foramen). These internal/external armature details are critical for species diagnoses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gemmule arrangement and attachment
rubrics_metrics.description: The gemmules are 'firmly adherent to the support of the sponge, at the base of which they are congregated in groups of four or more. They vary considerably in size and shape, many of them being asymmetrical and some elongate and sausage-shaped.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record position on sponge (base vs other surfaces), degree of aggregation, attachment mode, and shape variability (asymmetry, elongation); these features help distinguish species and infer reproductive ecology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of birotulate spicules with gemmules
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes: 'The fact that birotulate spicules are often found in close association with them, is particularly noteworthy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence/absence and frequency of birotulate spicules near gemmules is an important diagnostic character; document association and relative abundance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative/differential diagnostic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons such as: 'The main difference... between the typical African form and the Burmese variety consists in the former having much larger microstrongyles... Judging from Prof. Weltner's sections of gemmules, these bodies lack the definite outer shell of smooth macrostrongyles... A further difference consists in the presence, in the African specimen, of slender, finely spined strongyles [amphistrongyli], these being absent in the Burmese form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differences in spicule size/ornament, presence/absence of particular spicule classes (macrostrongyles, amphistrongyli), and gemmule armature as explicit differential characters when delimiting varieties/species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitat and environmental context (sponges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Field notes: specimen encrusted a lock-gate beam tarred several times; submerged from November to May eight hours/day at spring tides and dry during neap tides; from May to October constantly submerged; water at the lock always fresh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record substrate, anthropogenic treatments (e.g., tarred wood), tidal exposure and submersion regime, and salinity; use habitat data to interpret morphological variation and distribution, and as part of species accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmentally induced morphological variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed differences: lake specimens free from mud formed small pale crusts with raised conical oscula; specimens from very muddy running water formed broad black sheets that were markedly corrugated and had a harder skeleton.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that external form, colour, and skeleton firmness can vary with environment (mud content, flow conditions); do not rely solely on such plastic traits for species delimitation without corroborating internal characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical distribution and locality records
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: 'This sponge has only been found in the Western Ghats of the Bombay Presidency. Localities:--Igatpuri Lake and the R. Godaveri at Nasik.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record precise localities and broader distribution; geographic restriction or endemism is important in species accounts and may aid identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coelenterata defining structural criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Coelenterates are 'distinguished... by possessing a central cavity (the coelenteron or "hollow inside") the walls of which are the walls of the body and consist of two layers of cells separated by a structureless... jelly. This cavity has as a main function that of a digestive cavity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of a bi-layered body-wall with mesogloea and a central digestive cavity as a primary phylum-level diagnostic trait; document layer structure and functions in descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrozoa life-history (alternation of generations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Hydrozoa 'the primitive central cavity is not divided... In many species and genera the life-history is complex, illustrating what is called the alternation of generations... only alternate generations attain sexual maturity, those that do so being produced as buds from a sexless generation... The sexual forms as a rule differ considerably in structure from the sexless ones; many medusæ are the sexual individuals in a life-cycle in which those of the sexless generation are sedentary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record presence/absence and morphology of polyp vs medusa generations; note whether medusoid generation is suppressed (important for systematic placement) and differences in sexual vs asexual forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydra gross morphology and parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Hydra described as 'consisting of the following parts:--(1) an upright (or potentially upright) column or body, (2) a circle of contractile tentacles at the upper extremity of the column, (3) an oral disk or peristome surrounding the mouth and surrounded by the tentacles, and (4) a basal or aboral disk at the opposite extremity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe and illustrate body column, tentacle number/arrangement, oral disk, and basal disk; tentacle hollowness and contractility are diagnostic functional/anatomical notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body-wall layers and cell-type characters (Hydra)
rubrics_metrics.description: The body-wall consists of (i) ectoderm—outer cellular layer with muscle-, gland-, nerve-, and sense-cells; (ii) mesogloea—thin intermediate jelly; (iii) endoderm—internal layer with large polygonal cells, amoeboid inner surface, sometimes cilia and intracellular digestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document presence/appearance/functions of ectodermal, mesogloeal, and endodermal cells (muscle fibrils, gland cells, nerve-cells, cilia), since these are used in anatomical descriptions and physiological inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nettle-cells (cnidoblasts) structure and types
rubrics_metrics.description: A nettle-cell consists of (1) a true cell (the cnidoblast) which contains (2) a delicate capsule full of liquid; (3) a long thread coiled up in the capsule; and (4) a cnidocil or sensory bristle. 'In Hydra the nettle-cells are of two distinct types, in one of which the thread is barbed at the base, whereas in the other it is simple.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe nettle-cell ultrastructure, enumerate types (barbed vs simple threads), note associated nerve-cells, relative sizes (barbed capsules larger), and spatial distribution (more numerous in tentacles). These are key characters for species biology and systematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture and ingestion mechanism (Hydra)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prey contacting tentacles becomes paralysed by nematocyst discharge; 'the two kinds of threads have different functions... barbed threads penetrate... simple threads... wrap themselves round the more slender parts.' Adhesion aided by gummy ectoderm secretion; prey is brought to mouth by tentacle/column/peristome contractions and mucus from gastral cavity assists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing feeding biology, record types of nematocyst discharge, roles of barbed vs simple threads, adhesive secretions, mechanics of prey transport to mouth, and examples (e.g., Cyclops tail with wrapped simple threads and a penetrating barbed thread).

rubrics_metrics.name: Digestion (Hydra)
rubrics_metrics.description: After engulfment 'some digestive fluid is apparently poured out... soluble parts are dissolved out, the insoluble parts... being ejected. Digestion is, however, to a considerable extent intracellular, for the cells of the endoderm have the power of thrusting out... lobular masses... in which minute nutritive particles are enveloped and dissolved. The movements of the cilia... keep the food in the gastral cavity in motion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe both extracellular and intracellular digestion, ciliary mixing, retention location within gastral cavity, typical digestion time (several days in Calcutta form), and nature of excreta (flocculent mass).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colouration causes and environmental effects (Hydra)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In Hydra viridis... the green colour is due to the presence in the cells of green corpuscles... representing a stage in the life-cycle of Chlorella vulgaris.' In other species colour 'is largely dependent on food' or due to amorphous particles acting as food-reserve; starvation/temperature can cause loss of colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record pigment/corpuscle identity (symbiotic algae vs food-reserve particles), test reaction to starvation/temperature, and caution when using colour as a taxonomic character because it may be environmentally or trophically determined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviour and locomotion (Hydra)
rubrics_metrics.description: Species differ in locomotion: 'H. viridis progresses by "looping" like a geometrid caterpillar... H. vulgaris... bends down its column... stretches out its tentacles, detaches its basal disk, and then contracts the tentacles.' All species are attracted by light (but Calcutta H. vulgaris repelled by heat) and none move in a straight line; some show rhythmical contractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record mode of progression (looping, crawling), response to light/heat, rhythmical contractile behaviour, and movement frequency/directionality; behavioural traits can aid species/phase identification and experimental design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduction modes and timing (Hydra)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproduction occurs (i) by buds, (ii) by eggs, and (iii) occasionally by fission. Sexual organs (ovaries and spermaries) may occur on same individual; breeding seasons vary (temperate spring/winter, Calcutta February–March) and unfavourable conditions favour male development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document reproductive mode present, timing/seasonality, sexual system (monoecious vs dioecious tendencies), and environmental triggers (starvation, temperature, oxygen). Detail gametogenesis and gonad morphology for taxonomic accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budding pattern and tentacle development
rubrics_metrics.description: Buds 'arise as hollow outgrowths from the wall of the column, probably in a definite order and position in each species.' There is dispute on the order of tentacle appearance; number of initial tentacles can vary with brood/season (e.g., summer brood five, winter brood four in Calcutta H. vulgaris).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing budding, note positional regularity, sequence of tentacle formation, and brood-dependent variation; such developmental patterns have been used to propose species distinctions (Haacke).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fission and regeneration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Fission may be transverse or vertical (equal or unequal). 'It appears that, even in favourable circumstances, for a fresh polyp to be formed by artificial fission it is necessary for the piece to contain cells of both cell-layers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe mode of fission, typical initiation (constriction or elongation of oral disk), and crucially, regenerative requirement that fragments must include both ectodermal and endodermal cell layers to regenerate a complete polyp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egg development and fertilization (Hydra)
rubrics_metrics.description: The egg 'is said to be fertilized as it lies at the base of the ectoderm, through which the fertilizing spermatozoon bores its way.' After extrusion a chitinous egg-shell and inner membrane form; segmentation yields a hollow embryo which escapes by disintegration of the shell and rupture of the membrane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document site/timing of fertilization (within ectoderm), egg extrusion process (cup of elongated ectoderm cells), egg-shell composition, timing of segmentation and larval escape; these developmental details inform life-history and experimental embryology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enemies and parasitism
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Hydra seems to have few natural enemies' but recorded attackers include the minute worm Microstoma lineare and midge larvae that can devour H. vulgaris in Calcutta tanks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note documented predators/parasites, frequency and ecological context (e.g., midge larvae in tanks); include such records in ecological and conservation notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occurrence of marine coelenterates in brackish water
rubrics_metrics.description: Marine coelenterates 'not infrequently make their way or are carried by the tide up the estuaries... several species have been found living in isolated lagoons and pools of which the water was distinctly salt or brackish.' Example species lists (Bimeria vestita, Syncoryne filamentata, Irene ceylonensis, Sagartia schilleriana) and notes on medusoid suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record instances of estuarine/lagoonal occurrences, species identities, presence/absence of medusoid generation, and note adaptations (e.g., suppressed medusoid stage or morphological changes like burrowing in Sagartia schilleriana) when compiling faunal lists.
